questions.q: According to the lesson, which part of the six-part business brief is the single most powerful thing you can add to a prompt?
options: Constraints on length, tone and what to avoid
One or two examples of what 'good' looks like
A detailed description of the goal and success
A precise output format, such as a table
questions.explain: The lesson calls examples, one or two samples of 'good,' the single most powerful thing you can add to a prompt.

questions.q: A property manager asks AI to draft a lease renewal letter, but her notes don't include the new rent amount. Under the lesson's [CHECK] rule, what should the AI do?
options: Estimate a typical rent increase based on the local market
Leave the rent out and avoid mentioning any change at all
Use last year's rent, since it's the closest known figure
Write [CHECK] where the rent belongs instead of guessing
questions.explain: The [CHECK] rule tells the AI to use only the information provided and write [CHECK] where something is missing or unclear, so the gap is easy to find and fix before anything goes out.

questions.q: A gym owner's prompt 'Write a welcome email for new members' keeps producing generic drafts. Which change best applies the lesson?
options: Ask the AI to make the email longer and more enthusiastic
Run the same prompt several times until one sounds right
Add the goal, context, constraints, format and a past email he liked
Switch to a different AI assistant for all customer emails
questions.explain: The lesson says vague delegation gets vague work; a full brief with goal, context, inputs, constraints and format, plus an example of 'good,' produces usable output.
